{{smaller|'''Vermilion border''', the red part of the human lips, where the skin passes over into mucous membrane.—'''Vermilion flycatcher''', a small tyrant-bird of the genus ''Pyrocephalus'', as ''P. rubineus'', about 6 inches long, the male of which is dark-brown with all the under parts and a full globular crest vermilion-red or crimson. A bird of this kind inhabits Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, California, and the regions southward; and several others are found in the warmer parts of America. See cut under ''Pyrocephalus''.—'''Vermilion lacquer.''' Same as ''coral lacquer'' (which see, under ''coral'').}}

'''vermilion''' (vėr-mil′yo̤n), ''v. t.'' [< ''vermilion'', ''n.''] To color with or as with vermilion; dye red; cover or suffuse with a bright red.
{{smaller block|A sprightly red ''vermilions'' all her face.
{{right|''Granville'', A Receipt for Vapours.}}}}

'''vermily†''' (vėr′mi-li), ''n.'' [Irreg. extended from ''vermil'', ''vermeil''.] Same as ''vermilion''. ''Spenser'', F. Q., III. viii. 6.

'''vermin''' (vėr′min), ''n.'' [Formerly also ''vermine'' (also dial. ''varmin'', ''varmint'', ''varment''); < ME. ''vermine'', ''vermyne'', < OF. (and F.) ''vermine'' = Pr. ''vermena'' = It. ''vermine'', vermin, noxious insects, etc., as if < L. *''vermineus'' or *''verminus'', < ''vermis'', a worm: see ''worm''.] '''1.''' Any noxious or troublesome animal: mostly used in a collective sense.
{{smaller block|<poem>Your woful moder wende stedfastly
That cruel houndes or som foul ''vermyne''
Hadde eten yow. ''Chaucer'', Clerk’s Tale, l. 1039.</poem>}}
{{smaller block|(''a'') A worm; a reptile.
<poem>No heart have you, or such
As fancies, like the ''vermin'' in a nut,
Have fretted all to dust and bitterness.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, vi.}}}}

'''vernacularization''' (vėr-nak″ụ̄-lạ̈r-i-zā′shọn), ''n.'' [< ''vernacularize'' + ''-ation.''] The act or process of making vernacular; the state of being made vernacular.

{{smaller block|Thousands of words and uses of words, on their first appearance or revival as candidates for ''vernacularization'', must have met with repugnance, expressed or unexpressed.
{{right|''F. Hall'', Mod. Eng., p. 105.}}}}

'''vernacularize''' (vėr-nak′ụ̄-lạ̈r-īz), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''vernacularized'', ppr. ''vernacularizing''. [< ''vernacular'' + ''-ize.''] To make vernacular; vernaculate.

'''vernacularly''' (vėr-nak′ụ̄-lạ̈r-li), ''adv.'' In accordance with the vernacular manner; in the vernacular.

'''vernaculate''' (vėr-nak′ụ̄-lāt), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''vernaculated'', ppr. ''vernaculating''. [< L. ''vernaculus'', native, + ''-ate''<sup>2</sup>.] To express in a vernacular idiom; give a local name to. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|Very large Antwerp [red raspberry] “patches,” as they are ''vernaculated'' by the average fruit-grower.
{{right|''New York Semi-weekly Tribune'', July 15, 1887.}}}}

'''vernaculous†''' (vėr-nak′ụ̄-lus), ''a.'' [= Sp. ''vernáculo'' = Pg. It. ''vernaculo'', < L. ''vernaculus'', native, domestic, of or pertaining to home-born slaves: see ''vernacular''.] '''1.''' Vernacular.

{{smaller block|Their ''vernaculous'' and mother tongues.
{{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Tracts, viii.}}}}

'''2.''' Of or belonging to slaves or the rabble; hence, scurrilous; insolent; scoffing. [A Latinism.]

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|vermilion|6731|vernal}}</noinclude>{{smaller block|wax, and for other purposes. The name ''artificial vermilion'' is also applied to a vermilion red made by precipitating the coal-tar color eosin on orange mineral. It is quite equal in color, brilliancy, and body to that made from quicksilver; but it is not very permanent under the direct action of the sun, unless protected by a coat of varnish.}}
'''3.''' A color such as that of the above pigment; a beautiful brilliant red color.
{{smaller block|<poem>The armes, that earst so bright did show,
Into a pure ''vermillion'' now are dyde.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. v. 9.}}}}
'''4.''' A cotton cloth dyed with vermilion.
{{smaller block|They buy Cotton Wooll in London, that comes first from Cyprus and Smyrna, and at home worke the same, and perfit into Fustians, ''Vermilions'', Dymities, and other such Stuffes, and then returne it to London.
{{right|''L. Roberts'', Treasure of Trafikke, quoted in A. Barlow’s [Weaving, p. 26.}}}}
'''5.''' Same as ''vermeil'', 4.
{{smaller block|Several Gold Rings set with Turky and ''Vermillions''.
{{right|Quoted in ''Ashton’s'' Social Life in Reign of Queen [Anne, I. 181.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Antimony vermilion.''' See ''antimony.''—'''Orange vermilion.''' See ''orange''<sup>1</sup>.}}

'''II.''' ''a.'' Of the color of vermilion; of the brilliant pure-red color common in the bloom of the single scarlet geranium: as, a ''vermilion'' dye.
{{smaller block|<poem>The land of tears gave forth a blast of wind,
And fulminated a ''vermilion'' light,
Which overmastered in me every sense,
And as a man whom sleep hath seized I fell.</poem>
{{right|''Longfellow'', tr. of Dante’s Inferno, iii. 134.}} '''Vermilion border''', the red part of the human lips, where the skin passes over into mucous membrane.—'''Vermilion flycatcher''', a small tyrant-bird of the genus ''Pyrocephalus'', as ''P. rubineus'', about 6 inches long, the male of which is dark-brown with all the under parts and a full globular crest vermilion-red or crimson. A bird of this kind inhabits Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, California, and the regions southward; and several others are found in the warmer parts of America. See cut under ''Pyrocephalus''.—'''Vermilion lacquer.''' Same as ''coral lacquer'' (which see, under ''coral'').}}

'''vermilion''' (vėr-mil′yo̤n), ''v. t.'' [< ''vermilion'', ''n.''] To color with or as with vermilion; dye red; cover or suffuse with a bright red.
{{smaller block|A sprightly red ''vermilions'' all her face.
{{right|''Granville'', A Receipt for Vapours.}}}}

'''vermily†''' (vėr′mi-li), ''n.'' [Irreg. extended from ''vermil'', ''vermeil''.] Same as ''vermilion''. ''Spenser'', F. Q., III. viii. 6.

'''vermin''' (vėr′min), ''n.'' [Formerly also ''vermine'' (also dial. ''varmin'', ''varmint'', ''varment''); < ME. ''vermine'', ''vermyne'', < OF. (and F.) ''vermine'' = Pr. ''vermena'' = It. ''vermine'', vermin, noxious insects, etc., as if < L. *''vermineus'' or *''verminus'', < ''vermis'', a worm: see ''worm''.] '''1.''' Any noxious or troublesome animal: mostly used in a collective sense.
{{smaller block|<poem>Your woful moder wende stedfastly
That cruel houndes or som foul ''vermyne''
Hadde eten yow. ''Chaucer'', Clerk’s Tale, l. 1039.</poem>}}
{{smaller block|(''a'') A worm; a reptile.
<poem>No heart have you, or such
As fancies, like the ''vermin'' in a nut,
Have fretted all to dust and bitterness.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, vi.}} (''b'') A noxious or disgusting insect, especially a parasite; particularly, a louse, a bedbug, or a flea. (''c'') A mammal or bird injurious to game, and mischievous or troublesome in game-preserves: chiefly an English usage. Such quadrupeds as badgers, otters, weasels, polecats, rats, and mice, and such birds as hawks and owls, are all called ''vermin''.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Inhuman devill! think some fatall hower
Will bring huge troupes of ''vermine'' to devoure
Thy graine & thee.</poem>
{{right|''Times' Whistle'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 99.}}
They [of Java Major] feede on Cats, Rats, and other ''vermine''. {{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 540.}}
Like a ''vermin'' or a wolf, when their time comes they die and perish, and in the mean time do no good.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Holy Living, i. 1.}}
It is not so much to me and my fraternity as those base ''vermin'' the Otters. {{right|''I. Walton'', Complete Angler, p. 21.}}}}
Hence —'''2.''' A contemptible or obnoxious person; a low or vile fellow; also, such persons collectively.
{{smaller block|You are my prisoners, base ''vermine.''
{{right|''S. Butler'', Hudibras, II. iii. 1072.}}
Sir, this ''vermin'' of court reporters, when they are forced into day upon one point, are sure to burrow in another.
{{right|''Burke'', Amer. Taxation.}}}}

'''vermin†''' (vėr′min), ''v. t.'' [< ''vermin'', ''n.''] To rid or clear of vermin.
<poem>Get warrener bound
To ''vermine'' thy ground.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Tusser'', Husbandry, January’s Abstract.}}}}

'''verminate''' (vėr′mi-nāt), ''v. i.''; pret. and pp. ''verminated'', ppr. ''verminating''. [< L. ''verminare'', have worms, have crawling pains (cf. ''vermina'', gripes, belly-ache), < ''vermis'', worm: see ''vermin''.] To breed vermin; become infested with worms, lice, or other parasites.

'''vermination''' (vėr-mi-nā′shọn), ''n.'' [< L. ''verminatio(n-)'', worms (as a disease), also crawling pains, < ''verminare'', have worms, have crawling pains: see ''verminate''.] The generation or breeding of worms or other parasites; parasitic infestation, as by intestinal worms; helminthiasis; phthiriasis; the lousy disease.

'''verminer†''' (vėr′mi-nėr), ''n.'' A terrier.
{{smaller block|The beagles, the lurchers, and lastly, the ''verminers'', or, as we should call them, the terriers.
{{right|''Ainsworth'', Lancashire Witches, iii. 1.}}}}

'''vermin-killer''' (vėr′min-kil″ėr), ''n.'' One who or that which kills vermin.

'''verminly†''' (vėr′min-li), ''a.'' [< ''vermin'' + ''-ly''<sup>1</sup>.] Like or characteristic of vermin.
{{smaller block|They have nothing in them but a ''verminly'' nimbleness and subtlety, being bred out of the putrefactions of men’s brains. ''Bp. Gauden'', Hieraspistes (1653), p. 379. (''Latham.'')}}

'''verminous''' (vėr′mi-nus), ''a.'' [= F. ''vermineux'' = Sp. Pg. It. ''verminoso'', < L. ''verminosus'', full of worms, < ''vermis'', worm: see ''vermin''.] '''1.''' Tending to verminate, or breed vermin; affected with vermination; infested with parasitic vermin: as, ''verminous'' carrion.
{{smaller block|''Verminous'' and polluted rags dropt over-worn from the toyling shoulders of Time. ''Milton'', Prelatical Episcopacy.

Or how long he had held ''verminous'' occupation of his blanket and skewer. ''Dickens'', Tom Tiddler’s Ground, i.}}
'''2.''' Due to the presence of vermin; caused by vermin: as, ''verminous'' ulcers. See ''phthiriasis''. —'''3.''' Of the nature of or consisting of vermin; like vermin.
{{smaller block|<poem>Do you place me in the rank of ''verminous'' fellows,
To destroy things for wages?</poem>
{{right|''Middleton and Rowley'', Changeling, iii. 4.}}
<poem>That soft class of devotees who feel
Reverence for life so deeply that they spare</poem>}}
{{smaller block|The ''verminous'' brood.
{{right|''Wordsworth'', The Borderers, ii.}}}}

{{smaller block|''Verminous'' and murderous muckworm of the Parisian Commune. ''Swinburne'', Fortnightly Rev., N. S., XLII. 176.}}

{{smaller|'''Verminous crasis†''', a diseased condition supposed to be due to the presence of intestinal worms.—'''Verminous fever''', a fever due to the presence of intestinal worms.}}

'''verminously''' (vėr′mi-nus-li), ''adv.'' In a verminous manner, or to a verminous degree; so as to breed worms; as if infested by worms: as, ''verminously'' unclean.

'''vermiparous''' (vėr-mip′a̤-rus), ''a.'' [< L. ''vermis'', worm, + ''parere'', bear, + ''-ous''.] Producing or breeding worms.

{{smaller block|A generation of eggs, or some ''vermiparous'' separation.
{{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Vulg. Err., iii. 20.}}}}

'''vermis''' (vėr′mis), ''n.''; pl. ''vermes'' (-mēz). [L., a worm: see ''worm''.] In ''anat.'', the median lobe or division of the cerebellum; the vermiform process of the cerebellum, divided into ''prevermis'' and ''postvermis''.

'''Vermivora''' (vėr-miv′ọ-rä), ''n.'' [NL. (Swainson, 1827), < L. ''vermis'', a worm, + ''vorare'', devour.] A genus of birds, the American worm-eating warblers: now divided into several other genera, including ''Helmintherus'' (''Helinaia'' or ''Helonæa'') and ''Helminthophaga'' (or ''Helminthophila''). {{smaller|(See ''warbler'', ''swamp-warbler'', and cut under ''Helminthophaga''.) The name was applied by Lesson in 1831 to a different genus (of the family ''Tyrannidæ''), and had been used by Meyer in 1822 in another sense.}}

'''vermivorous''' (vėr-miv′ọ̄-rus), ''a.'' [< L. ''vermis'', worm, + ''vorare'', devour, + ''-ous''.] Worm-eating; feeding on worms; devouring grubs; erucivorous; campophagous.

'''Vermonter''' (vėr-mon′tėr), ''n.'' [< ''Vermont'' (see def.) + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] A native or an inhabitant of Vermont, one of the New England States of the United States of America.

{{smaller block|In 1776 the ''Vermonters'' sought admission to the provincial Congress.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XXIV. 168.}}}}

'''vermuth, vermouth''' (vėr′möth), ''n.'' [= F. ''vermout'', ''wermouth'', < G. ''wermuth'', wormwood, = AS. ''wermōd'', wormwood: see ''wormwood''.] A sort of mild cordial consisting of white wine flavored with wormwood and other ingredients. {{smaller|It is prepared chiefly in France and Italy, that of Turin being the most esteemed, and its special use is to stimulate the appetite by its bitterness.}}

'''vernacle<sup>1</sup>''' (vėr′na̤-kl), ''n.'' [< L. ''vernaculus'', native, vernacular: see ''vernacular''.] A vernacular word, term, or expression. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|''Vernacles'' or vernacular terms.
{{right|''Buck’s Handbook of Med. Sciences'', VIII. 518.}}}}

'''vernacle<sup>2</sup>†''' (vėr′na̤-kl), ''n.'' A Middle English form of ''vernicle''.

'''vernacular''' (vėr-nak′ụ̄-lär), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< L. ''vernaculus'', native, domestic, indigenous, of or pertaining to home-born slaves, < ''verna'', a native, a home-born slave (one born in his master’s house), lit. ‘dweller,’ < √ ''vas'' = Skt. √ ''vas'', dwell: see ''was''.] '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Native; indigenous; belonging to the country of one’s birth; belonging to the speech that one naturally acquires: as, English is our ''vernacular'' language. The word is always, or almost always, used of the native language or ordinary idiom of a place.

{{smaller block|This [Welsh] is one of the fourteen ''vernacular'' and independent Tongues of Europe, and she hath divers Dialects.
{{right|''Howell'', Letters, ii. 55.}}}}

{{smaller block|The tongues which now are called learned were indeed ''vernacular'' when first the Scriptures were written in them.
{{right|''Evelyn'', True Religion, I. 367.}}}}

{{smaller block|An ancient father of his valley, one who is thoroughly ''vernacular'' in his talk.
{{right|''De Quincey'', Style, ii.}}}}

'''2.''' Hence, specifically, characteristic of a locality: as, ''vernacular'' architecture.—'''Vernacular disease''', {{smaller|a disease which prevails in a particular country or district; an epidemic, or more accurately an endemic, disease.}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' One’s mother-tongue; the native idiom of a place; by extension, the language of a particular calling.

{{smaller block|He made a version of Aristotle’s Ethics into the ''vernacular.''
{{right|''Prescott'', Ferd. and Isa., i. 2.}}}}

{{smaller block|The English Church . . . had obtained the Bible in English, and the use of the chief forms of prayer in the ''vernacular.''
{{right|''Stubbs'', Medieval and Modern Hist., p. 261.}}}}

{{smaller block|On the bar we found friends that we had made in Panama, who had preceded us a few days, long enough to speak the ''vernacular'' of mining, and to pride themselves on being “old miners.”
{{right|''The Century'', XLII. 128.}}}}

'''vernacularism''' (vėr-nak′ū-lär-izm), ''n.'' [< ''vernacular'' + ''-ism.''] '''1.''' A vernacular word or expression. ''Quarterly Rev.''—'''2.''' The use of the vernacular: the opposite of ''classicalism.''

'''vernacularity''' (vėr-nak-ū-lar′i-ti), ''n.''; pl. ''vernacularities'' (-tiz). [< ''vernacular'' + ''-ity.''] A vernacularism; an idiom.

{{smaller block|Rustic Annandale, . . . with its homely honesties, rough ''vernacularities.''
{{right|''Carlyle'', Reminiscences (Edward Irving), p. 264.}}}}

'''vernacularization''' (vėr-nak″ụ̄-lạ̈r-i-zā′shọn), ''n.'' [< ''vernacularize'' + ''-ation.''] The act or process of making vernacular; the state of being made vernacular.

{{smaller block|Thousands of words and uses of words, on their first appearance or revival as candidates for ''vernacularization'', must have met with repugnance, expressed or unexpressed.
{{right|''F. Hall'', Mod. Eng., p. 105.}}}}

'''vernacularize''' (vėr-nak′ụ̄-lạ̈r-īz), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''vernacularized'', ppr. ''vernacularizing''. [< ''vernacular'' + ''-ize.''] To make vernacular; vernaculate.

'''vernacularly''' (vėr-nak′ụ̄-lạ̈r-li), ''adv.'' In accordance with the vernacular manner; in the vernacular.

'''vernaculate''' (vėr-nak′ụ̄-lāt), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''vernaculated'', ppr. ''vernaculating''. [< L. ''vernaculus'', native, + ''-ate''<sup>2</sup>.] To express in a vernacular idiom; give a local name to. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|Very large Antwerp [red raspberry] “patches,” as they are ''vernaculated'' by the average fruit-grower.
{{right|''New York Semi-weekly Tribune'', July 15, 1887.}}}}

'''vernaculous†''' (vėr-nak′ụ̄-lus), ''a.'' [= Sp. ''vernáculo'' = Pg. It. ''vernaculo'', < L. ''vernaculus'', native, domestic, of or pertaining to home-born slaves: see ''vernacular''.] '''1.''' Vernacular.

{{smaller block|Their ''vernaculous'' and mother tongues.
{{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Tracts, viii.}}}}

'''2.''' Of or belonging to slaves or the rabble; hence, scurrilous; insolent; scoffing. [A Latinism.]

{{smaller block|The petulancy of every ''vernaculous'' orator.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Volpone, Ded.}}}}

'''vernage†''' (vėr′nāj), ''n.'' [< ME. ''vernage'', < OF. ''vernage'', < It. ''vernaccia'', “a kind of strong wine like malmesie or mukadine or bastard wine” (Florio, 1598) (ML. ''vernachia''), lit. ‘winter wine,’ < ''vernaccio'', a severe winter, < ''verno'', winter, = It. Pg. ''inverno'' = Sp. ''invierno'' = F. ''hiver'', winter, < L. ''hibernus'', pertaining to winter: see ''hibernate''.] A kind of white wine.
{{smaller block|<poem>He drynketh ypocras, clarree, and ''vernage'',
Of spices hoote, to encressen his corage.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Merchant’s Tale, l. 563.}}
Sche brougthe hem ''Vernage'' and Crete.
{{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 111, Index.}}}}

'''vernal''' (vėr′nal), ''a.'' [< F. ''vernal'' = Pr. Sp. Pg. ''vernal'' = It. ''vernale'', < LL. ''vernalis'', of the spring, vernal, < L. ''ver'', spring: see ''ver''.] '''1.''' Of or pertaining to the spring; belonging to the spring; appearing in spring: as, ''vernal'' bloom.
{{smaller block|In those ''vernal'' seasons of the year, when the air is calm and pleasant, it were an injury and sullenness against Nature not to go out and see her riches.
{{right|''Milton'', Education.}}
The ''vernal'' breeze that drives the fogs before it, . . . if augmented to a tempest, will . . . desolate the garden.
{{right|''Goldsmith'', National Concord.}}
<poem>And beg an alms of spring-time, ne’er denied
Indoors by ''vernal'' Chaucer.</poem>
{{right|''Lowell'', Under the Willows.}}}}
'''2.''' Of or belonging to youth, the springtime of life.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
